anchorData: Constants: use pi = 22/7 everywhere. 1 cm³ = 1 mL; 1000 cm³ = 1 L; 1 m³ = 1000 L = 1,000,000 cm³. KERICHO CONTAINERS (all about 60 cm tall, opening diameter 42 cm, so opening radius 21 cm): (A) Cylindrical drum: r = 21 cm, h = 60 cm, V = (22/7) x 21 x 21 x 60 = 83,160 cm³ = 83.16 L. (B) Conical sisal cover: r = 21 cm, h = 60 cm, V = 1/3 x 83,160 = 27,720 cm³ = 27.72 L. (C) Metal frustum bucket: top radius R = 21 cm, bottom radius r = 14 cm, h = 60 cm, V = 1/3 x (22/7) x 60 x (441 + 294 + 196) = 1/3 x (22/7) x 60 x 931 = 58,520 cm³ = 58.52 L. Ordering: cone 27.72 L < bucket 58.52 L < cylinder 83.16 L. Cylinder = exactly 3 x cone (83.16 / 27.72 = 3). Bucket is about 70% of the cylinder (58.52/83.16 = 0.7037) and about 2.11 x the cone. Bucket as cones: bottom radius 14, top radius 21, so the ratio is 2:3 and the missing small cone has h = 120 cm; the full cone has h = 180 cm. Large cone (r = 21, h = 180) = 1/3 x (22/7) x 441 x 180 = 83,160 cm³. Small cone (r = 14, h = 120) = 1/3 x (22/7) x 196 x 120 = 24,640 cm³. Difference = 58,520 cm³ (matches the frustum formula). PYRAMID GRAIN-STORE MODEL (Lesson 3): square base side 30 cm, height 40 cm; matching cuboid 30 x 30 x 40 = 36,000 cm³; pyramid = 1/3 x 900 x 40 = 12,000 cm³ = 12 L. FRUSTUM-OF-PYRAMID MAIZE BIN MODEL (Lesson 5): top square side 60 cm (A1 = 3,600 cm²), bottom square side 30 cm (A2 = 900 cm²), sqrt(A1 x A2) = 1,800 cm², height 40 cm. V = 1/3 x 40 x (3,600 + 900 + 1,800) = 1/3 x 40 x 6,300 = 84,000 cm³ = 84 L. Check: large pyramid (side 60, h 80) = 96,000 cm³ minus small pyramid (side 30, h 40) = 12,000 cm³ = 84,000 cm³. Maize bulk density = 0.75 kg per litre, so the bin holds 84 x 0.75 = 63 kg maize. LESSON 6 PROBLEM DATA: (1) Turkana conical water tank: radius 1.4 m, height 3 m, V = 1/3 x (22/7) x 1.96 x 3 = 6.16 m³ = 6,160 L. (2) Githeri frustum pot: top radius 30 cm, bottom radius 24 cm, height 35 cm; R² + Rr + r² = 900 + 720 + 576 = 2,196; V = 1/3 x (22/7) x 35 x 2,196 = 80,520 cm³ = 80.52 L; 100 people at 0.5 L each = 50 L, which fits in the pot. (3) Frustum cup: top radius 6 cm, bottom radius 3 cm, height 7 cm; V = 1/3 x (22/7) x 7 x (36 + 18 + 9 = 63) = 462 cm³; the Kericho cylindrical drum (83,160 cm³) holds 83,160 / 462 = 180 cups. LESSON 7: learner-made models have their own measured values; expect measured volume within about 5-10% of the calculated volume because of card thickness, imperfect shapes and spilled water or sand.
characters: Mama Chebet: tea farmer in Kericho who owns the cylindrical drum, conical cover and bucket; she compares them side by side. Mr. Kiprop: her neighbour who carries leaves in the metal bucket to the weighing station and asks why the bucket is not as big as the drum. Kericho tea farmers' collection point and weighing station: where the three containers are used, in Kericho County. Cylindrical drum (A), woven sisal conical cover (B), metal frustum bucket (C): all about 60 cm tall with a 42 cm opening; use the exact data in anchorData. Turkana homestead family: needs a conical water tank (Lesson 6). Githeri pot: used for a 100-person community meal in Nairobi (Lesson 6). Pyramid grain-store models: used in Lessons 3 and 5 for maize storage in Rift Valley. Ms. Wanjiru: the class teacher in the story. Learners work in groups; the DQB (Driving Question Board) is posted on the classroom wall.
outcome: The three containers look alike because they share the same height and opening radius (21 cm, 60 cm), but their shapes are different, and shape determines volume. The cone holds exactly one third of the cylinder (27.72 L against 83.16 L) because V(cone) = 1/3 x pi x r² x h. The bucket is a frustum, which is a large cone (83.16 L, r = 21 cm, h = 180 cm) with a small cone (24.64 L, r = 14 cm, h = 120 cm) removed, so it holds 58.52 L, between the cone and the cylinder. The same reasoning for pyramids and their frustums lets learners design a frustum container of any required capacity.
conventions: Use pi = 22/7 in all calculations unless a lesson says otherwise. Volume = space inside a solid (cm³, m³); capacity = amount a container can hold (mL, L). Conversions: 1 cm³ = 1 mL; 1000 cm³ = 1 L; 1 m³ = 1000 L. Symbols: r = radius (small end), R = radius (large end), h = perpendicular (vertical) height (never the slant height), A1 and A2 = areas of the two parallel faces. Formulas by name: cylinder V = pi r² h; cone V = 1/3 pi r² h; pyramid V = 1/3 x base area x height; frustum of a cone V = 1/3 pi h (R² + Rr + r²); frustum of a pyramid V = 1/3 h (A1 + A2 + sqrt(A1 A2)). 'Frustum' always means the solid left when the top of a cone or pyramid is cut off parallel to the base. Containers are called drum (A), cover (B) and bucket (C) in every lesson. Quote litres to 2 decimal places for the Kericho containers. Maize bulk density = 0.75 kg/L. Phases in each lesson: Predict, Observe, Explain, DQB, Model Building. The class model is a single cumulative diagram that grows each lesson.

lessonMap.teaches: Launch of the Kericho containers puzzle: learners predict and estimate which of the drum, cover and bucket holds most, and revise units of volume versus capacity (cm³, m³, mL, L) with conversions.
lessonMap.buildsOn: No earlier lesson; builds on Junior School volume of prisms and unit conversion.
lessonMap.usesData: The three Kericho containers (A, B, C) with 60 cm height and 42 cm opening; unit conversions in the constants. Do NOT reveal the actual capacities.

lessonMap.teaches: Volume of a cone, V = 1/3 pi r² h, discovered by pouring (cone fills the cylinder exactly three times) and applied to calculate capacity.
lessonMap.buildsOn: Lesson 1 (predictions, unit conversion, the DQB question about the drum versus the cover).
lessonMap.usesData: Drum A = 83.16 L and cover B = 27.72 L; ratio exactly 3.

lessonMap.teaches: Volume of a pyramid, V = 1/3 x base area x height, from the 3-to-1 relation of cuboid to pyramid, and converting to capacity.
lessonMap.buildsOn: Lesson 2 (the one-third relationship from cone and cylinder; Lesson 1 predictions revisited).
lessonMap.usesData: Pyramid grain-store model: side 30 cm, h 40 cm, cuboid 36,000 cm³, pyramid 12,000 cm³ = 12 L.

lessonMap.teaches: Deriving V = 1/3 pi h (R² + Rr + r²) by subtracting the small cone from the large cone (similar triangles to find the missing height); resolving the phenomenon by finding the bucket's capacity.
lessonMap.buildsOn: Lesson 2 (cone formula) and Lesson 3 (one-third idea); Lesson 1 predictions about the bucket.
lessonMap.usesData: Bucket C: R 21, r 14, h 60; large cone h 180 = 83,160 cm³, small cone h 120 = 24,640 cm³, bucket 58.52 L; comparison with drum A and cover B.

lessonMap.teaches: Volume of a frustum of a pyramid, V = 1/3 h (A1 + A2 + sqrt(A1 A2)), and using density to convert capacity to mass of maize.
lessonMap.usesData: Maize bin model: A1 3,600, A2 900, h 40, V = 84,000 cm³ = 84 L, mass 63 kg at 0.75 kg/L.

lessonMap.teaches: Choosing the correct formula and unit conversion in multi-step Kenyan word problems, including dividing one capacity by another (number of cups per drum).
lessonMap.buildsOn: Lessons 2-5 (all four formulas) and Lesson 1 (unit conversions).
lessonMap.usesData: Lesson 6 problem data: Turkana tank 6,160 L; githeri pot 80.52 L; cup 462 cm³ and 180 cups per drum A.

lessonMap.teaches: Designing and constructing model containers, measuring dimensions, calculating theoretical volume, verifying by filling with water or sand, and analysing percentage error and its causes.
lessonMap.usesData: Learners' own measurements; anchorData formulas only; expected error about 5-10%. Reference Kericho figures are used only for comparison of shape.

lessonMap.teaches: Synthesising the relationships among cylinder, cone, pyramid and frustum into one annotated diagram; explaining the final outcome of the phenomenon; assessing all five specific learning outcomes.
lessonMap.buildsOn: Lessons 1-7 (all formulas, project results, DQB and cumulative model).
lessonMap.usesData: All Kericho container data (83.16 L, 27.72 L, 58.52 L; 3:1 ratio; large cone 83,160 cm³ minus small cone 24,640 cm³); learners' Lesson 1 predictions compared with actual values.
